unit.title: Global Challenges, Society and Sustainable Futures

theory.title: Global Institutions, Cooperation and Conflict
theory.explanation: This C2 mission examines global institutions, cooperation and conflict. Analyse competing interests, distinguish evidence from assumption and recognise how institutional choices distribute risks and benefits. Strong responses qualify claims, define terms precisely and acknowledge uncertainty without becoming evasive.
theory.tip: Name the mechanism, identify who benefits or bears the cost, and qualify conclusions in proportion to the evidence.

patterns.label: Define the issue
patterns.pattern: Specify the system, population and time frame under discussion.
examples: The proposed multilateral target applies to public buildings by 2035.

patterns.label: Interrogate evidence
patterns.pattern: Separate measured outcomes from projections and causal explanations.
examples: The association is consistent across districts, although it does not establish causation.

patterns.label: Map distribution
patterns.pattern: Ask how costs, access and risks differ across groups.
examples: The aggregate improvement conceals persistent gaps in peripheral neighbourhoods.

patterns.label: Recommend proportionately
patterns.pattern: Link an actionable recommendation to a measurable review point.
examples: The measure should be piloted, independently evaluated and revised after twelve months.

content.passage: Negotiators seeking a regional agreement on water security faced competing claims over sovereignty, infrastructure funding and emergency access. Earlier meetings had stalled because each delegation treated concessions as evidence of weakness. A mediator reframed the discussion around shared risks: drought, damaged infrastructure and the costs of unilateral action. The resulting framework did not settle every dispute, but it established data-sharing protocols, an emergency notification mechanism and a timetable for reviewing allocation rules. Observers described the agreement as limited but meaningful. Its legitimacy would depend on whether smaller communities could participate and whether commitments were monitored consistently. The case illustrated that multilateral cooperation rarely removes conflicting interests; it creates procedures through which those interests can be negotiated.
